newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala Congress votes controversial amnesty law.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala Congress votes controversial amnesty law.

text.p: The Guatemalan Congress on Wednesday overwhelmingly approved an amnesty law that opponents fear will let people responsible for massacres go unpunished.

The government of President Alvaro Arzu had promoted the law as part of the leadup to a definitive peace treaty to be signed between the government and leftist rebels on Dec. 29. That agreement will end a 36-year-old civil war that has left 140,000 Guatemalans dead or "disappeared."

The so-called National Reconciliation Law passed on its third reading, with 65 votes in favour, 8 votes against and 7 members absent. Congress was closed to the general public during the debate to keep out protestors.

"My father died (during the war), and to this day we don't know who is responsible. But even so, this leads me to accept that if the people of Guatemala want reconciliation, we have to learn to forgive," Congressman Vinicio Villar Anteu of the Christian Democratic Party said as he voted for the bill.
"Because of the blood left by my father and also my first husband, I'm voting against the law," Congresswoman Rosalina Tuyuc of the New Guatemala Democratic Front (FDNG) said.

Under the terms outlined in the law and in a peace accord signed by the government and guerrillas in Madrid last week, guerrilla fighters will not be prosecuted for political crimes such as rebellion and sedition.

Guerrillas and army personnel will also receive amnesty for common crimes -- involving, for example, threats, property damage, fires, explosives or falsification of documents -- as long as they were clearly connected to the course of the war.

The amnesty law contains a clause excluding from amnesty crimes against humanity, but it does not specify what those are. Guatemala has not signed the Geneva Convention, which defines "crimes against humanity."
Controversy over the clause was acute because of the many government army massacres of peasants carried out during the brutal counterinsurgency campaigns of the 1980s.

Human rights activists argued further that the bill did not specifically exclude kidnappings and murders from crimes that would receive amnesty. They said they feared that army officers accused of ordering the murder of political opponents and intellectuals would never stand trial.
A few leftist members of Congress raised their voices against the law on Wednesday, but all their proposed amendments were voted down.
The Alliance Against Impunity, a group of prominent human rights activists opposed to amnesty, protested outside the legislature after lawmakers voted to bar the general public.
